description: The title track of Steel Pulse's fifth album, released in January 1984 on their own Wise Man Doctrine label. David Hinds turns Cold War dread, famine and racism into an urgent roots-reggae warning that still sounds timely.

pops.text: Title track alert: 'Earth Crisis' opens Side B of Steel Pulse's fifth studio album, released in January 1984 on the band's own Wise Man Doctrine label.
Every track on the album was written by frontman David Hinds — lead singer, guitarist and the band's primary songwriter since the beginning.
Steel Pulse formed in 1975 at Handsworth Wood Boys School in Birmingham, England — Hinds, Basil Gabbidon and Ronald McQueen were schoolmates.
The spark? Hinds and Gabbidon were inspired to start the band after hearing Bob Marley and the Wailers' 'Catch a Fire.'
The song opens with a declaration: 'The Earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof' — scripture repurposed as an environmental alarm bell.
Check the album cover: Ronald Reagan, Soviet leader Yuri Andropov and Pope John Paul II all stare out from the artwork.
That cover later named a band — metalcore group Earth Crisis took their name from this album, citing its images of famine, Cold War blocs and Klansmen.
The album was recorded at Jacobs Studios in Farnham and Horizon Studios in Coventry, with Jimmy Haynes co-producing.
Chart report: 'Earth Crisis' the album peaked at No. 154 on the Billboard 200 and No. 34 on the Dutch Albums Chart.
The album's opener, 'Steppin' Out,' earned Steel Pulse a Grammy nomination for Best Reggae Recording.

title: Earth Crisis

description: Track two on 'Babylon the Bandit,' the album that won Steel Pulse a Grammy. A joyful, pointed history lesson arguing that Black people and African origins were written out of familiar Bible translations.

pops.text: This is track two on 'Babylon the Bandit' — right after the opener 'Save Black Music,' so the album's mission statement arrives early.
The hook says it plainly: 'A dis ya version, a no King James version — 'cause out of Africa came the Garden of Eden.'
David Hinds wrote it. The song takes exception to the absence of Black people in most versions of the Bible.
Its roll call names Daniel, King David and Abraham, presenting the ancient prophets as 'black and bold.'
'Babylon the Bandit' was produced by Jimmy 'Senyah' Haynes and was the band's most polished, synth-centered record to date.
Label tension: Elektra had been steering Steel Pulse toward a pop-reggae sound like Eddy Grant's — this anthem pushed proudly the other way.
Grammy history: 'Babylon the Bandit' won Best Reggae Album, making Steel Pulse the first non-Jamaican act ever to win that award.
That distinction lasted decades — the album held it until American band SOJA won the category in 2022.
The sessions were recorded in 1985, with new faces Carlton Bryan on guitar and Alvin Ewen on bass replacing founding members who had left.
Still a live staple: David Hinds performed it in his 2025 Goa Sunsplash set in India, nearly 40 years after it was recorded.

title: Not King James Version

description: Steely Dan's breakthrough single and the opening track of their 1972 debut 'Can't Buy a Thrill.' A Latin-tinged tale of gamblers and repeat offenders, carried by an electric sitar and a very unusual 'plastic organ.'

pops.text: Opening track, opening statement: this opens Steely Dan's debut album 'Can't Buy a Thrill,' released in November 1972.
Written by Walter Becker and Donald Fagen, produced by Gary Katz, and recorded in August 1972 at the Village Recorder in Santa Monica.
Odd credit: on the original 1972 release, this Becker-Fagen original was credited as 'Trad' — for traditional.
That swirling solo is an electric sitar, played by Denny Dias — who later left music and became a computer programmer.
The second solo is Fagen on what the liner notes call a 'plastic organ' — a Yamaha YC-30 with a sliding pitch-bending ribbon.
Radio got a shorter edit: the single version trims the intro and outro and omits the organ solo — 4:14 versus 5:56 on the album.
Chart climb: it debuted on the Billboard Hot 100 on November 18, 1972, and peaked at No. 6 in February 1973.
It remains Steely Dan's second highest-charting single, behind only 'Rikki Don't Lose That Number.'
Two singers, one song: Fagen sings the album version, but David Palmer fronted the band live and sang it on 'The Midnight Special' in February 1973.
Afterlife: Waylon Jennings, Tori Amos and Smash Mouth have all covered it, and it turned up in the 2008 game 'Guitar Hero World Tour.'

title: Do It Again

description: The second single from 'Can't Buy a Thrill,' a bouncy kiss-off famous for Elliott Randall's one-take guitar solo — the solo Jimmy Page called his favorite of all time. It peaked at No. 11 in 1973.

pops.text: That guitar fireworks display in the first seconds? That's session player Elliott Randall — and he wasn't even a member of Steely Dan.
Randall knew Becker and Fagen from earlier days playing in the backing band for Jay and the Americans and on their early demos.
Jeff 'Skunk' Baxter was first assigned the lead guitar part; when it wasn't landing to the band's satisfaction, Randall was asked to give it a try.
One take. Randall's entire lead — intro, answers, solo and end solo — was recorded in a single continuous take, with no edits or punch-ins.
His simple setup: his old Strat plugged straight into an Ampeg SVT amp, miked with a single AKG 414.
Randall recalled an unrecorded run-through the band loved — the tape wasn't rolling. The keeper that followed was still just one take.
Jimmy Page rated this solo his favorite of all time — and scored it 12 out of a possible 10.
Guitar World readers agreed, sort of: in 2016 they ranked it the 40th best guitar solo of all time.
Released as a single in March 1973, it peaked at No. 11 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 7 on the Cash Box Top 100.
Hunt down the four-channel quadraphonic mix if you can — it contains extra lead guitar fills not heard in the familiar stereo version.

title: Reelin' In The Years

description: The closing track of Sting's 1985 solo debut 'The Dream of the Blue Turtles.' A song of appeasement after a broken marriage, built on medieval imagery — and a chorus Sting counted among his best.

pops.text: Closing track: this ends Sting's debut solo album 'The Dream of the Blue Turtles,' released on June 17, 1985.
Sting wrote it in a Barbados recording studio in 1985, working with modal chords on guitar that he thought sounded 'kind of medieval.'
Hence the siege imagery — castle walls, trenches and barbed wire as a metaphor for a struggling romantic relationship.
Sting told Musician magazine it's about appeasement: you lay a minefield to protect someone, then realize you have to walk back through it.
He also said, 'I think it's one of the best choruses I've ever written.' Hard to argue.
That soaring saxophone is Branford Marsalis, star of the jazz band Sting assembled for the album with Kenny Kirkland, Darryl Jones and Omar Hakim.
Chart split: No. 8 on the US Billboard Hot 100, but only No. 49 in Sting's native UK.
On Billboard's Top Rock Tracks it did even better — No. 1 for two weeks, his second consecutive No. 1 on that chart.
It was the album's second single in the US and third in the UK; the B-side in Europe was 'Shadows in the Rain.'
Stage prank: at an early Paris performance, his crew lowered a tiny fortress onto the stage — a parody of the Stonehenge scene in 'This Is Spinal Tap.'

title: Fortress Around Your Heart

description: Sting's first solo single and the opening track of his 1985 debut album The Dream of the Blue Turtles. A jazz-tinged pop song written as the antidote to The Police's possessive 'Every Breath You Take.'

pops.text: Solo liftoff: this was Sting's first single away from The Police, and it opens his debut solo album, The Dream of the Blue Turtles.
Sting wrote it as a deliberate foil to 'Every Breath You Take' — where that song was about surveillance and possession, this one says: if you love somebody, let them alone.
An early demo of the song was recorded with a handy session guest: Phil Collins.
For his solo band Sting auditioned New York jazz players — Branford Marsalis on sax, Kenny Kirkland on keyboards, Darryl Jones on bass and Omar Hakim on drums.
The album sessions spent seven weeks at Eddy Grant's Blue Wave Studio in Barbados, with mixing afterwards at Le Studio in Quebec.
The video was directed by Godley & Creme in Paris. Each musician was filmed separately on a soundstage, then the performances were overlaid into one band.
The B-side was 'Another Day.' The 12-inch single went clubbier, with remixes by John 'Jellybean' Benitez and a 'Torch Mix' by William Orbit.
It peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 and spent three weeks at No. 1 on Billboard's Album Rock Tracks chart. In the UK it reached No. 26.
At the 1995 Brit Awards, Sting duetted on it with M People's Heather Small — backed by a 100-strong gospel choir at Earls Court.
Freedom ages well: a dance re-recording for his 2019 album My Songs, produced by Dave Audé, topped Billboard's Dance Club Songs chart that September.

title: If You Love Somebody Set Them Free

description: A relentless funk workout from Talking Heads' 1980 album Remain in Light, built on African polyrhythms and looping grooves with producer Brian Eno. David Byrne delivers one of rock's earliest rap-like vocals.

pops.text: Track two on Remain in Light, released October 8, 1980 — Talking Heads' fourth album, and their third and final one produced by Brian Eno.
It was never a regular US single: it came out as a promotional single in America in 1980, then as a proper single in Germany in 1981.
The band recorded it in July and August 1980 at Compass Point Studios in the Bahamas, building the instrumental tracks as a series of looping grooves.
The template was Fela Kuti: Eno introduced the band to the Nigerian Afrobeat pioneer's music, and African polyrhythms drive the whole track.
Guitarist Adrian Belew recorded his parts for this track in a single day, leaning on effects units and a Roland guitar synthesizer.
That's Nona Hendryx of Labelle adding backing vocals — one of several extra musicians who expanded the four-piece for these sessions.
That rapid-fire 'Facts are simple and facts are straight' section? Chris Frantz played Byrne Kurtis Blow's 'The Breaks' to inspire the rap-like delivery.
The 1981 video, directed by Toni Basil, doesn't show the band at all — at their request. Street dancers do the work, and the video mix adds a verse the LP version doesn't have.
Talking Heads trusted it with the biggest moment: 'Crosseyed and Painless' is the closing song of their landmark 1984 concert film Stop Making Sense.
Phish covered all of Remain in Light as their Halloween 'musical costume' in 1996 — and kept this song in their live rotation ever after, stretching it past 20 minutes.

title: Crosseyed and Painless

description: Talking Heads' biggest US hit, released in July 1983 as the first single from Speaking in Tongues. A funk-fuelled jam that grew out of a Parliament-Funkadelic audience chant and David Byrne's nonsense syllables.

pops.text: Released in July 1983, this was the first single from the band's fifth album, Speaking in Tongues.
It started as a jam between the rhythm section — bassist Tina Weymouth and drummer Chris Frantz, who are also married.
Frantz had just seen Parliament-Funkadelic at Madison Square Garden and kept yelling their audience chant, 'Burn down the house!' Byrne liked it and stretched it to 'Burning down the house.'
Byrne's lyric method, borrowed from Brian Eno: chant nonsense syllables over the groove until the phrasing fits, then find real words to match it.
Roads not taken: phrases Byrne tried and dropped included 'I have another body,' 'I'm still under construction' — and, for the chorus, 'Foam Rubber, USA.'
Byrne directed the video himself. The house in it stands on Myrtle Street in Union Township, New Jersey, and younger lookalikes puppeteer the band members into playing.
The video ends with an extended close-up of Byrne's face projected onto a dark two-lane highway at night, the broken centre line running through it.
It peaked at No. 9 on the Billboard Hot 100 — Talking Heads' only US Top 10 single. Yet in the UK it didn't chart at all, and in Australia it stopped at No. 94.
A year later, an extended live version became a highlight of the concert film Stop Making Sense, whose remaster returned to IMAX screens for its 40th anniversary in 2023.

Cover karma: Tom Jones and the Cardigans took it to No. 7 in the UK in 1999, and Paramore led the 2024 Stop Making Sense tribute album with their version — Byrne returned the favour by covering Paramore's 'Hard Times.'

title: Burning Down the House

description: The Belgian hip-house anthem that took dance music mainstream, released August 18, 1989. Producer Jo Bogaert built it on a house classic, Ya Kid K rapped it — and a model who didn't sing became its first face.

pops.text: A Belgian export: Technotronic was producer Jo Bogaert's project, and on this record he's credited under his producer alias, Thomas de Quincey.
The voice and the lyrics are Ya Kid K — born Manuela Barbara Kamosi Moaso Djogi, a Congolese-Belgian rapper Bogaert built the track around.
But the woman in the video isn't her. Model Felly Kilingi lip-syncs throughout and fronted the first album cover — a marketing tactic. Ya Kid K got the cover on a later repackaging.
Billboard later noted Bogaert built the track on a dancefloor classic: Marshall Jefferson's Chicago house landmark 'Move Your Body.'
That relentless beat leans on a house-music staple, the Roland TR-909 drum machine — Roland's own history of the song singles it out.
Lyric check: Bogaert says most people sing 'I want a place to stay,' but Ya Kid K actually sings 'Awa, a place to stay' — 'awa' meaning home.
Released August 18, 1989, it went to No. 1 in Belgium, Finland, Iceland, Portugal and Spain — and No. 2 in the UK.

So close in America: it hit No. 2 on the Hot 100 and No. 1 on the dance chart, and went Platinum. Billboard noted it had the week's top sales points, but Michael Bolton's airplay lead kept it off No. 1.
It's often cited as the first Eurodance song to become a hit in the US, and an early landmark of hip house — rap fused with deep house.
It refuses to leave: a D.O.N.S. remix topped the British Dance Chart in 2005, and the video became a running gag in the 2022 mockumentary series Cunk on Earth.

title: Pump Up The Jam

description: Technotronic's sleeper hit: recorded in 1989 for their debut album, then resurrected as a single in 1992 after Revlon put it in TV commercials. It became the Belgian project's third and final US Top 10 hit.

pops.text: Old song, new life: this was recorded in 1989 and already sat on Technotronic's debut album, Pump Up the Jam: The Album, years before it was a hit.
Ya Kid K co-wrote the lyrics with producer Jo Bogaert, who produced the track — she's the featured voice throughout.
Patience pays: it wasn't released as a single until 1992, three years after the album version first appeared.
The trigger was lipstick. Billboard's Larry Flick wrote in 1992: 'Resurrection via a Revlon TV commercial has sparked heavy pop radio interest.'
The commercial did its job: the single peaked at No. 6 on the Billboard Hot 100, becoming Technotronic's third and final US Top 10 hit.
The music video was directed by the Kahn Brothers — though the official upload used here is the licensed Topic audio, not that clip.
Critics heard sunshine in it: The Morning Call called it 'a sunny blend of subtle African world beat and house music,' while Knight Ridder heard a '60s female-group sound with a house update.
A re-recorded version was included on Technotronic's The Greatest Hits, released in 1993.
Screen life: the song turns up in the Will Arnett and Dax Shepard film Let's Go to Prison and in the King of the Hill episode 'Dances with Dogs.'
Still moving: in 2017 BuzzFeed ranked 'Move This' No. 35 in its list of the 101 Greatest Dance Songs of the '90s.

title: Move This

description: A slow-burning soul ballad from Tedeschi Trucks Band's 2011 debut Revelator, with Susan Tedeschi's aching vocal wrapped around Derek Trucks' singing slide guitar. It became the young band's signature song.

pops.text: Track three on Revelator, released June 7, 2011. It was the debut album from an 11-piece band that had only formed the year before.
Written by Derek Trucks with vocalist Mike Mattison. Mattison had been the lead singer in Trucks' previous outfit, the Derek Trucks Band.
Revelator was recorded at Swamp Raga, Derek and Susan's own studio in Jacksonville, Florida, and co-produced by Trucks with Jim Scott.
Fans heard this one early: the band previewed it live at Eric Clapton's Crossroads Guitar Festival in Chicago in 2010, a year before the album.
Comedian Bill Murray, the Crossroads host that day, introduced the band before that festival performance, which was preserved on the festival DVD.
The band is a family business: leaders Derek Trucks and Susan Tedeschi married in 2001 and built this group together in 2010.
Revelator won the Grammy Award for Best Blues Album at the 54th Grammys, quite a first impression for a debut record.
Trucks joined the Allman Brothers Band in 1999, following his uncle Butch Trucks, a founding Allman drummer. The slide-guitar lineage runs deep.
Mattison later cut his own version for his 2014 solo album You Can't Fight Love, giving the song a second, Stax-flavoured life.
In 2016 the band played it at the Apollo Theater, in Harlem itself, during the release week for their album Let Me Get By. Right song, right room.

title: Midnight in Harlem

description: Tedeschi Trucks Band's warm, uplifting 2022 tribute to their late keyboardist and flutist Kofi Burbridge, from I Am The Moon: IV. Farewell. A goodbye that chooses celebration over sorrow, groove over grief.

pops.text: This is a loving tribute to Kofi Burbridge, the band's original keyboardist and flutist, who died in February 2019 at age 57.
Keyboardist Gabe Dixon had the idea of writing about Kofi, and co-wrote the song with Derek Trucks and vocalist Mike Mattison.
Dixon joined the band in 2018, at first filling in while Burbridge was ill, which makes his tribute to his predecessor especially touching.
Kofi's partnership with Trucks ran deep: he joined the Derek Trucks Band in 1999 and was Trucks' longest-running musical collaborator.
He was classically trained, born in the Bronx in 1961, and played keyboards, organ and flute, also arranging strings for the band.
Kofi's brother is bassist Oteil Burbridge of the Allman Brothers Band and Dead & Company. Both brothers were in Tedeschi Trucks Band's first line-up.
Burbridge died on February 15, 2019, the very day the band's album Signs, his final album with them, was released.
The song arrived in August 2022 on I Am The Moon: IV. Farewell, the closing chapter of a four-album, 24-song project with four companion films.
That whole project grew from a 12th-century Persian poem, Layla and Majnun by Nizami Ganjavi, suggested to the band by Mattison during the pandemic.
Percussionist Marc Quinones, Trucks' old Allman Brothers bandmate, adds congas, and the band played the song on Jimmy Kimmel Live! that August. Kofi's rhythm, still moving them.

title: Soul Sweet Song

description: The opening track and a single from The Black Crowes' 1990 debut Shake Your Money Maker, all Stones-y swagger and slide guitar. Brothers Chris and Rich Robinson announcing themselves at full volume.

pops.text: This is track one on Shake Your Money Maker, the band's debut, released February 13, 1990 on Def American. First impressions matter, and this is a loud one.
Written by brothers Chris and Rich Robinson, like nearly everything on the album. Chris sings it, Rich drives it on guitar.
Released as a single at the end of 1990, it reached No. 11 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart, just missing the top 10.
The album peaked at No. 4 on the Billboard 200 and sold more than five million copies, still the band's best-seller.
Quiz answer: the album is named after a classic blues song by Elmore James, a song that is not actually on the album.
The Robinsons started out in 1984 as Mr. Crowe's Garden, formed while they were still in high school in Marietta, Georgia.
Producer George Drakoulias spotted them at a New York show in 1988, got them signed to Def American, then produced this record.
Executive producer Rick Rubin's name was left off the original sleeve and only added after the album became a hit. Success has its perks.
This is the band's only album with guitarist Jeff Cease. Marc Ford replaced him in time for the follow-up record.
Director Pete Angelus shot the video in a mansion, the band playing at night, then shown at a daytime lunch during the guitar solo. Rock and roll, with lunch.

title: Twice As Hard

description: The lead single from The Black Crowes' chart-topping 1992 second album The Southern Harmony and Musical Companion, a gospel-tinged rocker about freedom that ruled rock radio for eleven weeks at No. 1.

pops.text: Track two on The Southern Harmony and Musical Companion, and its lead single, released April 20, 1992, ahead of the album on May 12.
It reached No. 1 on Billboard's Album Rock Tracks chart in May 1992 and stayed there for 11 straight weeks.
On the pop chart it peaked at No. 48 on the Hot 100, while in Britain it reached No. 24, the band's highest-charting UK single.
Chris Robinson told Songfacts the song is about freedom, written in response to the war on drugs, which he called a silly concept.
The original single's B-side was 'Darling of the Underground Press', a deep cut title worth the price of the 45 alone.
Its parent album debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 and went double platinum, the band's first chart-topping album.
The album was cut remarkably fast, in about eight days at Southern Tracks in Atlanta, with most songs done in one or two takes.
That album title comes from an 1835 hymnal, The Southern Harmony, and Musical Companion, compiled by Baptist song leader William Walker.
It was the first Crowes album with guitarist Marc Ford and full-time keyboardist Eddie Harsch, a line-up change you can hear throughout.
Four singles from the album topped the rock chart, a record run, and Pete Angelus, who directed 'Twice As Hard', directed this video too.

title: Remedy

description: A silky, harmony-stacked single from Nashville-via-Birmingham indie-soul band The Brook & The Bluff, released in March 2021 ahead of their second album Yard Sale. Warm, wistful and impeccably sung by all four members.

pops.text: Released as a single on March 5, 2021, months before the album arrived. A little advance taste of Yard Sale.
Yard Sale came out in stages, Side A in April and the full album on October 8, 2021, a deliberate vinyl feel for the streaming era.
The album was produced by Micah Tawlks, the band's longtime collaborator, who has also worked with COIN and Jake Wesley Rogers.
It was a featured single from the album alongside 'Doobie Bronson', two very different song titles, one very smooth band.
A misnomer is a wrong or misleading name, which is funny from a band whose own name needs explaining, see the next pop.
The name comes from their Birmingham, Alabama, pockets: Bluff Park for frontman Joseph Settine, Mountain Brook for the others. Brook, meet Bluff.
They are a four-piece built on four-part harmony: Settine, guitarist Alec Bolton, drummer John Canada and bassist Fred Lankford, and everybody sings.
Originally from Birmingham, the band is based in Nashville, Tennessee, and built its following the slow way, on the road.
Their debut album First Place (2019) introduced favourites like 'Halfway Up', 'Everything Is Just A Mess' and 'Shelby'.
The song stayed a live staple: their 35-date fall 2021 tour sold out rooms like New York's Bowery Ballroom, and 'Misnomer' was still opening a show in Wilmington in September 2025.

title: Misnomer
